articles.title: World: Victims of Trafficking in Human Beings in Asylum and Reception (Situational Update Issue No 26, 30 July 2026)
articles.description: Country: World Source: European Union Agency for Asylum Please refer to the attached file. The information presented in this Situational Update complements the developments reported in the Asylum Report 2026. It is a follow-up to Fact Sheet No 34, covering the period 1 July 2025-30 June 2026. EU legislation contains provisions which address asylum applicants with special needs who may be considered particularly vulnerable, including victims of human trafficking. These provisions ensure that vulnerable applicants receive adequate support to benefit from their rights and comply with the obligations, which are defined under the Common European Asylum System (CEAS). EU Member States were obligated to transpose the revised EU Anti-Trafficking Directive by 15 July 2026, which aims to address emerging challenges and strengthen strategic and operational responses to tackling human trafficking. One of the main requirements is to adopt a national action plan by 2028 to ensure a coordinated and sustainable response to human trafficking and establish formal referral mechanisms and national focal points for cross-border referral of victims In parallel, the entry into force of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum in June 2026 fostered the development of tools to strengthen early identification of vulnerable persons, including presumed trafficking victims, in asylum and reception systems and to have an effective national referral system.

articles.title: Republican inadvertently calls Trump's biggest success the 'scandal of my lifetime'
articles.description: A GOP senator accidentally called President Donald Trump's biggest success the "scandal of my lifetime" with his comments on Fox News. Sen. Ron Johnson spoke with Fox News on Wednesday about COVID vaccinations in light of the recent testimony by Anthony Fauci. He told anchor Laura Ingraham that "these injections cause death" and that the COVID vaccine is the "great government scandal of my lifetime." However, online critics noted that Trump boasted in the past that his first administration rolled out the COVID vaccines and that Johnson's comments amounted to calling Trump's success a scandal. "Trump literally said, 'I came up with the vaccines,'" progressive news personality Alex Cole wrote in a post on X. "If you believe Ron Johnson, then isn't he admitting Trump's biggest accomplishment was a disaster?" Democratic strategist Leslie Marshall similarly noted that Johnson was slamming COVID vaccines that "Trump green-lighted expeditiously." "He is a really dangerous liar. Who is he working for??" legal analyst Sara Dillon posted , mocking Johnson's attack on Fauci, who worked for the Trump administration during COVID. Others simply went after Ron Johnson's claims that COVID vaccines "cause death." "Ron Johnson needs a warning label," blogger Jim Stewartson wrote . "Having him on television is a risk to public health, an act of deadly negligence. FOX should be sued by everyone who lost someone because they listened to compromised idiots like this." "This isn't just political posturing: this is evil and will hurt innocent people," lawyer and political commentator John Jackson posted . "It's not enough to beat the Republican Party. We need to expose them so badly that they have to change their name."

articles.title: From bad to worse for Trump and his base
Democratic state lawmakers push to hold ICE accountable nationwide
articles.description:
A group of Democratic state lawmakers from around the nation were in Chicago Wednesday to push for more legislation that would give the public the ability to sue ICE agents over fatal shootings and arrests made without warrants.

“I never imagined that I would spend the majority of my first two years in my term drafting laws and helping support laws that protect people from our own federal government,” said state Sen. Graciela Guzman (D-Chicago) who led a news conference organized by an advocacy group known as State Innovation Exchange.

“I thought we'd be talking about lowering healthcare, lowering costs, funding our schools, and fighting for a more equitable Illinois. Instead, this (Trump) administration has forced states like ours into a different kind of work, which is defending our communities from federal overreach.”

Last fall, Illinois became among the few states in the country to allow residents to sue immigration agents who violate their constitutional rights to due process and protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.

House Bill 1312 was signed into law last fall. The law’s other key provision bans civil immigration arrests in and around Illinois courthouses.

Lawmakers from other states, including Georgia, Maryland, Utah, Colorado and Minnesota, said they also are pushing for protections for their residents.

“We have had federal agents break car windows and rain glass down on one-year-old children, or throw middle-aged women to the ground who were peacefully protesting,” said Colorado state Sen. Mike Weissman. “All of us up here are state legislators who deeply believe in using the power that we have under our constitution as states to simply try to make life more livable and more dignified for our constituents.”

The shooting deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota in January and now the targeting of immigrants with expired visas at U.S. airports are examples why state lawmakers have to move fast with legislation, said Minnesota state Sen. Omar Fateh.

Feteh, whose district is on the south side of Minneapolis, said he authored legislation in early 2024 to protect Minnesotans from the violation of their rights by immigration agents. But, he said his fellow lawmakers felt it was too soon, too politically risky and too hypothetical to pass.

“Beginning in late 2025, Trump sent 3,000 armed, masked, untrained agents to Minnesota. It was the largest federal invasion in American history in a state that has less than 1% of the nation's undocumented people. Trump's agents rounded up random people on the street, they arrested whole families, young children, moms, and old women," Feteh said.

"They pursued, harassed, detained, arrested, and jailed Minnesotans in every stage of immigration, including legal status, refugees, naturalized citizens, even second and third generation citizens, and then they killed two civilian observers, Renee Good and Alex Pretti,” Feteh added. “Suddenly, the fight to protect people from Trump's fascism went from being too early to seemingly too late."

Guzman, co-chair of the Illinois Latino Legislative Caucus, said five lawsuits have been filed under the new state law.

Michael Puente is a reporter and anchor for WBEZ. Reach him mpuente@wbez.org.
